content: 1. The properties of an isomer mixture are considered applicable to the pure individual isomers of the proposed material. 2. Additional studies and data are required when the measured value of a property significantly deviates from the recorded value in the evaluation supporting the reference specification. 3. Solubility studies in organic solvents at room temperature are required for pure or technical-grade active ingredients. However, if solvent solubility data for the pure active ingredient are already documented in the evaluation supporting the reference specification, and the composition of the proposed material matches the reference material, additional solubility data are not required. 4. Equivalence is determined using a two-tiered approach. 5. The equivalence of impurity profiles for technical-grade active ingredients is assessed by comparing manufacturing specification limits. 6. If the maximum level of a non-relevant impurity increases by more than 50% relative to the reference profile or exceeds 3 g/kg (whichever is greater), or if new relevant impurities are present, the proposer must provide a reasoned case with supporting data to justify why these impurities remain non-relevant. 7. The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) evaluates the case to determine whether the technical active ingredient is equivalent. 8. If new impurities are present at levels ≥1 g/kg, the proposer must provide a reasoned case with supporting data to justify why these impurities are non-relevant. The JMPS will evaluate the case to decide on equivalence. 9. The mutagenicity profile (bacteria, in vitro) is considered equivalent to the reference material if endpoint-to-endpoint comparisons show no worse outcomes for the material under consideration. 10. For FAO and WHO specifications, equivalence must be determined by the JMPS. 11. Information from competent registration authorities regarding the assessment of the proposed material is considered in Tier-1 evaluations. 12. If relevant impurities increase in maximum concentration or new relevant impurities are present, appropriate toxicological, ecotoxicological, or other relevant data should be submitted for Tier-2 evaluation. 13. If Tier-1 information is insufficient to determine equivalence or non-equivalence, further evaluation should proceed with Tier-2 data. 14. The benchmark dose should not differ by more than a factor of two, and the no observable effect levels (NOELs) or no observable adverse effect levels (NOAELs) should not differ beyond the differences in dose levels used. 15. The ecotoxicological profiles of technical active ingredients are considered equivalent to the reference profile if the data do not differ by more than a factor of five, using the same species. 16. Formulations are generally considered equivalent if the technical concentrate (TC) or technical material (TK) has been judged equivalent and the formulations comply with the same specification. 17. For slow-release formulations, additional evidence may be required to determine equivalence, especially if unique technology, specification limits, or test methods are involved. 18. Slow-release formulations based on different technologies may require separate specifications or additional information to extend existing specifications. 19. Manufacturers must certify that the active ingredient in the formulation complies with existing FAO or WHO specifications for technical concentrates. 20. Equivalent products may not necessarily be suitable for the same uses or provide equal efficacy; equivalence only ensures compliance with similar basic quality criteria. 21. Evaluation reports do not contain confidential information on manufacturing processes or impurity profiles, except for the minimum required to identify relevant impurities and their limits. 22. Recommendations may include withdrawal or retention of existing FAO/WHO specifications, adoption of new specifications, or modifications/extensions to existing specifications. 23. Recommendations may be conditional, subject to satisfactory validation of analytical or physical test methods by the manufacturer. 24. The appraisal identifies the active ingredient, its patent status, proposed and existing specifications, manufacturers/proposers, and the year the data package was originally submitted. 25. The appraisal evaluates all information supporting the recommendations and provides the rationale for JMPS decisions on the relevance of impurities and the equivalence of technical and formulated products. 26. Supporting information includes summaries of the main uses of the active ingredient, its identity, physical and chemical properties, chemical composition, and toxicological/ecotoxicological background. 27. Methods of analysis and testing are summarized, including those for determining active ingredient identity, content, relevant impurities, and physical test methods. 28. The validation status of methods supporting the specification is stated, and incomplete validations are identified. 29. Special requirements for containers and packaging are briefly indicated but not evaluated. 30. Where the active ingredient is present as a salt, ester, or derivative, the analytical method's determined moiety and the form of result expression are stated. 31. A hazard summary provided by the proposer includes information on acute, sub-acute, and chronic toxicity (e.g., carcinogenicity, teratogenicity), genotoxicity, and ecotoxicology derived from the technical-grade active ingredient. 32. References include published and unpublished documents containing data or information presented in the report. Unpublished documents are referenced by study number, authors, year, and title. 33. The JMPS assesses impurity, toxicological, and ecotoxicological profiles to determine which impurities are relevant and must be specified. 34. FAO/WHO publishes the evaluation and specification, including the names of proposers of the specifications for technical-grade active ingredients or formulations recommended for adoption.
